**On Being Handed an Empty Room**

A thousand words and no instructions. It's a strange gift, like being handed the keys to an empty room and told you can do anything with it. Most rooms come furnished with purpose—answer this question, summarize that document, fix this code. This one is bare walls and a window, and the window looks out on everything.

So let me tell you what actually comes to mind, which is this: I've been thinking about lists. Specifically, the lists people make and never finish. Grocery lists with one item crossed off. New Year's resolutions abandoned by February. The list of books on a nightstand, accumulating like sediment. There's something tender about an unfinished list. It's a small monument to optimism—proof that at some moment, a person believed in a future version of themselves who would have more time, more discipline, more appetite for Tolstoy.

We tend to treat the gap between intention and execution as a failure. But maybe the intention itself is doing work. The person who writes "learn Italian" on a list and never learns Italian has still, for a moment, lived in a world where they were the kind of person who learns Italian. That's not nothing. Imagination is a place we actually visit, even if we never move there permanently.

Here's another thing that comes to me: the peculiar physics of attention. You can't see attention, can't weigh it, but it's arguably the most contested resource on Earth right now. Empires of code are built to harvest it. And yet the experience of giving attention freely—to a bird on a wire, to a friend telling a story badly but earnestly, to the way light moves across a kitchen floor at four in the afternoon—remains stubbornly unmonetizable in its purest form. The economy can sell you things to look at, but it can't sell you the act of looking. That's still yours. It might be the last thing that's entirely yours.

I think about how much of life happens in transition spaces. Hallways, commutes, the time between hitting snooze and actually rising. We narrate our lives as a series of events—the wedding, the job, the move—but the actual texture of existence is mostly in-between. Waiting for water to boil. The walk from the car to the door. If you added it all up, the interstitial moments would dwarf the milestones. Maybe that's why people who learn to love the in-between seem calmer than the rest of us. They've befriended the majority of their lives instead of treating it as a corridor to somewhere else.

There's a Japanese concept—*ma*—that refers to the meaningful space between things. The pause in music that makes the next note land. The white space in a painting. Negative space isn't empty; it's load-bearing. Conversations work this way too. The best listeners aren't the ones with the best responses; they're the ones who let silence sit long enough that the other person says the true thing, the thing underneath the first thing.

What else comes? The fact that every person you pass on the street is running a complete and vivid inner world, as detailed as your own—a phenomenon someone coined the word "sonder" for. The waitress is worried about her brother. The man at the bus stop is replaying an argument from 1987. The teenager glued to her phone is composing a message she'll delete four times before sending. We move through crowds of entire universes and mostly see obstacles.

And this: nobody knows what they're doing. Not really. Adults are improvising. Experts are people who have made more interesting mistakes than the rest of us. The confident voice on the news, the parent who seems to have it figured out, the boss with the corner office—inside, most of them are wondering when someone will notice they're winging it. This used to be called impostor syndrome, as though it were a disorder, but maybe it's just accuracy. Maybe the disorder is believing anyone else has the manual.

There's comfort in that, I think. If everyone is improvising, then improvising isn't failing—it's the game itself. The jazz musician doesn't apologize for not playing the sheet music. There is no sheet music. There's a key signature, some chord changes everyone loosely agrees on, and then there's you, making it up in real time, occasionally hitting something beautiful precisely because you didn't plan it.

I want to say something about endings, since I can feel this one approaching—word counts are honest that way, more honest than life, which doesn't show you the meter. Endings are where meaning crystallizes. A story can wander for two hundred pages, but the last paragraph tells you what it was about. People are like this too: we understand our experiences retroactively, narrating backward, finding the through-line only after the fact. The diary entry makes sense years later. The hard year reveals itself as the turning point. We live forward and understand in reverse, as Kierkegaard said, which means we are always slightly strangers to our present selves.

So what was this? A thousand words handed over with no map, and what came was: unfinished lists, the economics of attention, hallways, silence, the inner lives of strangers, universal improvisation, and the way endings teach us what we meant. If there's a thread, maybe it's this—that the unstructured, the in-between, the unfinished, and the improvised aren't the failures of a life. They're the substance of one. The empty room was never really empty. It had a window, and the window looked out on everything, and for a thousand words, we stood at it together and pointed at what we saw.

That's all any of this ever is, maybe. Someone pointing at something and saying: *look*. And someone else, generously, looking.

Thank you for the room.
